messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stanc model name
messages.body_plain:
The name needs to be a valid C++ identifier so
that it can be the name of a class!  You may
want to fix this name and always use the same one
in the R interface so you know where to find it
from the R side.

See the discussion of valid identifiers on this
page:

   http://www.cplusplus.com/doc/tutorial/variables/

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] NUTS I vs II
messages.body_plain:
Ok, I've found what was causing this problem. It was a bug in the way
that command-line options were being parsed—there was a missing ! in
the line where adapt_epsilon was set, so a much-too-high fixed step
size was being used, and the sampler effectively wasn't sampling at
all. But each failed iteration was super-fast! I pushed the 1-line
fix.

Having fixed that bug, I wasn't able to reproduce the failing 1-d
normal bug, and turning on --unit_mass_matrix doesn't affect the
output when you keep the seed fixed. So hopefully it doesn't show up
again.

Best,
Matt

messages.subject: seed-related NaNs & sampling
messages.body_plain:
We have a problem with random inits on some seeds
in the BUGS/vol1/salm model.  For some seeds, the
first eval is NaN and Stan then continues to reject
and stay in NaN-land for the entire chain.

There's really no way we can escape a situation where
the first eval is NaN.

We could reseed, but I think we'd need to do this
deterministically (based on the initial seed;
say adding 1M to it) so that when given the seed
the next time, the sampler does the same thing.

For restarting, we're going to dump out a copy of
the current state (which when used as the seed next
time lets you start where you left off).

- Bob

messages.subject: reseeding for NaN cases
messages.body_plain:
Daniel and I just put in a patch that will try
random initialization up to 100 times if the random inits
do not lead to a finite log prob and to finite gradients for
all dimensions. (It's not checked in yet, but will be
in gm/command).

This approach will be repeatable under new seeds.

Does 100 seem like an OK number of attmepts?  They're actually
not that expensive compared to sampling, so we could set it
higher.  Or make it command-line configurable, I suppose.
(I want to resist adding new command-line options as much
as possible -- it makes it confusing to users -- maybe we
could tier them into basic and advanced if we need more.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] seed-related NaNs & sampling
messages.body_plain:
One easy way to reseed deterministically is to use a random integer drawn using the current seed as the new seed.

Alternatively, you could draw inits until the first eval isn't NAN before using it as a starting point for the Markov chain.  In fact, even if you reseed you'd still need to redraw the initial sample so you'd do this anyway and the reseeding is probably not necessary.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: diffuse inits -> low prob -> high gradients -> NaN
messages.subject_clean: diffuse inits -> low prob -> high gradients -> NaN
messages.body_plain:
(Marcus:  yes, you're absolutely right -- it's a model
problem.  And we'll never solve all of those.  You can
specify inits now in the command, but there's no good way
yet to specify them programatically -- it's on the to-do
list and we may set the summer student to writing and
testing the random generators we'll need.)

(Jiqiang:  you still only need a single seed;
we took the approach Marcus suggested.)

So here's the story:

With init retries, the BUGS vol1/salm model at least took off.
But it crashed after 12 iterations with NaN everywhere.

What appears to be happening (see below for a dump)
is that random inits in (-2,2) on the unconstrained scale can
lead to very small initial log probabilities (-1E34) and
very large gradients (1E34) even when the initial log prob
isn't NaN.  Finite diffs fail by returning zero (see below),
but the actual model gradients are all finite.

In contrast, all-zero inits work fine, with all-zero inits,
the log prob is -2E1 (yes, E1), and the biggest gradient is 1E5,
the maximum error from finite diffs is 1E-8 and everything runs
fine.

Daniel also brought up the problem that the random momenta
on the unit normal scale can cause problems, but those should
only lead to rejections if they're really badly tuned.  And
the varying step size (equivalently variable diagonal mass matrix)
should help.

I think we either need to

a) more agressively lower the step size in the sampler
    during warmup (but then it has to be allowed to creep back
    up when we get into higher probability regions), or

b) trim the init interval from (-2,2) to something much
    less agressive, say (-.25,.25).

We'll still run into problems if all-zero inits don't behave
well because we're initializing around them.  For the salm model,
the predictor vector x has values ranging from 0 to 1000.
The salm.stan model centers them, but doesn't rescale.
Presumably the Poisson's blowing out in exponentiating
the linear basis in the model (y[i,j] ~ poisson(exp(...)));
I don't see how to fix that by taking a log(lambda) as the
parameter instead of lambda -- you wind up needing to
exponentiate to calc the log probability anyway.

We'll have an issue if someone initializes a precision value
uniformly, as in

    tau ~ uniform(0,1000);
    sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau);

In this case, a 0-init on tau leads to 1/sqrt(500) = .04.
On the other hand,

    sigma ~ uniform(0,1000);

will start with sigma = 500, which is probably better
behaved than having the scale too low.

Of course, there's no way to solve our init problems
in general.  An adversarial model designer will still
be able to trash any general init scheme.

Here's the example from the salm model, with some ill-behaved
random inits:

messages.subject: still problems with mdivide_left_tri in g++ 4.2
messages.subject_clean: still problems with mdivide_left_tri in g++ 4.2
messages.body_plain:
Daniel and I have been struggling with a problem
in inv_wishart that only seems to arise in g++ 4.2.

It can't find mdivide_left_tri(X,Y) when X and Y
are matrices of var.

 From what we can tell, it *should* work through
argument-dependent lookup (that is, we think the
other compilers are right and g++ 4.2 is wrong).
Everything else seems to work OK that way.

Fix 1:  We were able to make it work by including
stan/agrad/matrix.hpp in stan/prob.../inv_wishart.hpp
and then adding a "using stan::agrad::mdivide_left_tri"
to the other using statements in the body of inv_wishart.

The problem is that we don't want dependencies from
the math lib to agrad.  We could just forget about all
that and rewrite all the probability functions to include
agrad.

Potential Fix 2: A brute-force patch that might work for this case
would be to include specializations of inv_wishart
in stan::agrad that would include the relevant
files.

Fix 3:  Tell people with Macs to use clang and take
the 10% or so performance hit.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] g++ 4.2, ADL, mdivide_left_tri, & partial template instantiation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] g++ 4.2, ADL, mdivide_left_tri, & partial template instantiation
messages.body_plain:
Wow, that's an annoying g++ bug.  Good work tracking it down.

I'd suggest adding inlined mdivide_left_tri_l and mdivide_left_tri_u and having them call mdivide_left_tri which would avoid duplicating code and should avoid the problem since the template parameters would be fully instantiated.

On Thu, Jun 7, 2012 at 2:05 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Yatta!  I isolated a simple test case, then
> figured out why multiply was different than
> mdivide_left_tri, and even have a sketch of a
> solution that works -- but it'll take a bit of
> work to refactor what's there and I'm out for
> the next few days.
>
> To make a long story short, the problem really
> does seem to be a bug in g++ 4.2's argument-dependent lookup:
>
>   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument-dependent_name_lookup
>
> Specifically, an interaction with partially specifying
> types during type inference and argument-dependent lookup.
>
> I started by isolating a minimal test case with the same error
> as we saw for the inv_wishart model compilation:
>
> --------------------
> #include <stan/math/matrix.hpp>
> #include <stan/agrad/matrix.hpp>
>
> int main() {
>  using stan::agrad::var;
>
>  Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen::Dynamic> I;
>  Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen::Dynamic> L;
>
>  // fails to compile w/o agrad;  with math, gives our warning message
>  using stan::agrad::mdivide_left_tri;
>  using stan::math::mdivide_left_tri;
>  L = mdivide_left_tri<Eigen::Lower>(L,I);
>
>  // works fine
>  L = multiply(I,L);
> }
> -----------------------
>
> I put the above in a file ~/stan/test.cc,
> made libstan.a, then did this:
>
>  ~/stan> g++ -O0 -Lbin -lstan -Isrc -Ilib test.cpp
>
> Everything compiles fine.  multiply() works even
> without the using statement.  That's what's supposed to happen
> with argument-dependent lookup.
>
> If you get rid of the using statement for agrad::mdivide_left_tri,
> you get the same error message we've been getting for inv_wishart
> in the tests with the long template lists.  But, if you get rid
> of the math::mdivide_left_tri using, you only get a function
> not found error.
>
> The question remains as to why mdivide_left_tri() doesn't work
> when multiply() does.  But if you look at the test cases in
> the code above, it's obvious -- there's  an explicit partial
> template instantiation in the call to mdivide_left_tri and
> none in multiply.
>
> So I took the original definition:
>
>    template<int TriView,int R1,int C1,int R2,int C2>
>    inline Eigen::Matrix<var,R1,C2> mdivide_left_tri(const Eigen::Matrix<var,R1,C1> &A,
>                                                     const Eigen::Matrix<var,R2,C2> &b) {
>      if (A.cols() != A.rows())
>        throw std::invalid_argument("A is not square");
>      if (A.cols() != b.rows())
>        throw std::invalid_argument("A.cols() != b.rows()");
>      return A.template triangularView<TriView>().solve(b);
>    }
>
> and added a variant with a hard-coded Eigen::Lower on the last line:
>
>    template <int R1,int C1,int R2,int C2>
>    inline Eigen::Matrix<var,R1,C2> mdivide_left_tri2(const Eigen::Matrix<var,R1,C1> &A,
>                                                      const Eigen::Matrix<var,R2,C2> &b) {
>      if (A.cols() != A.rows())
>        throw std::invalid_argument("A is not square");
>      if (A.cols() != b.rows())
>        throw std::invalid_argument("A.cols() != b.rows()");
>      return A.template triangularView<Eigen::Lower>().solve(b);
>    }
>
> I added
>
>    L = mdivide_left_tri2(L,I);
>
> to the test program, and Bob's your uncle.*
>
> Unfortunately, this hard-codes the view into the function.
> But if we want to run on g++ 4.2 (and it is the default
> with the usual Mac developer tools and so will probably
> be the defualt in R), I don't see an alternative
> at this point.
>
> Can we just hardcode triangularView for lower-triangular views
> for now?  If not, we can add both.  And there are all the
> other similar functions.
>
> - Bob
>
> * http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob's_your_uncle <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob%27s_your_uncle>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] diffuse inits -> low prob -> high gradients -> NaN
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] diffuse inits -> low prob -> high gradients -> NaN
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This was due to a bug in nuts_diag.hpp where it would estimate 0
variance for every dimension, leading to per-variable step sizes of
0/0=NaN. I'll push the fix later today.

Matt

On Wed, Jun 6, 2012 at 5:21 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> (Marcus:  yes, you're absolutely right -- it's a model
> problem.  And we'll never solve all of those.  You can
> specify inits now in the command, but there's no good way
> yet to specify them programatically -- it's on the to-do
> list and we may set the summer student to writing and
> testing the random generators we'll need.)
>
> (Jiqiang:  you still only need a single seed;
> we took the approach Marcus suggested.)
>
> So here's the story:
>
> With init retries, the BUGS vol1/salm model at least took off.
> But it crashed after 12 iterations with NaN everywhere.
>
> What appears to be happening (see below for a dump)
> is that random inits in (-2,2) on the unconstrained scale can
> lead to very small initial log probabilities (-1E34) and
> very large gradients (1E34) even when the initial log prob
> isn't NaN.  Finite diffs fail by returning zero (see below),
> but the actual model gradients are all finite.
>
> In contrast, all-zero inits work fine, with all-zero inits,
> the log prob is -2E1 (yes, E1), and the biggest gradient is 1E5,
> the maximum error from finite diffs is 1E-8 and everything runs
> fine.
>
> Daniel also brought up the problem that the random momenta
> on the unit normal scale can cause problems, but those should
> only lead to rejections if they're really badly tuned.  And
> the varying step size (equivalently variable diagonal mass matrix)
> should help.
>
> I think we either need to
>
> a) more agressively lower the step size in the sampler
>   during warmup (but then it has to be allowed to creep back
>   up when we get into higher probability regions), or
>
> b) trim the init interval from (-2,2) to something much
>   less agressive, say (-.25,.25).
>
> We'll still run into problems if all-zero inits don't behave
> well because we're initializing around them.  For the salm model,
> the predictor vector x has values ranging from 0 to 1000.
> The salm.stan model centers them, but doesn't rescale.
> Presumably the Poisson's blowing out in exponentiating
> the linear basis in the model (y[i,j] ~ poisson(exp(...)));
> I don't see how to fix that by taking a log(lambda) as the
> parameter instead of lambda -- you wind up needing to
> exponentiate to calc the log probability anyway.
>
> We'll have an issue if someone initializes a precision value
> uniformly, as in
>
>   tau ~ uniform(0,1000);
>   sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau);
>
> In this case, a 0-init on tau leads to 1/sqrt(500) = .04.
> On the other hand,
>
>   sigma ~ uniform(0,1000);
>
> will start with sigma = 500, which is probably better
> behaved than having the scale too low.
>
> Of course, there's no way to solve our init problems
> in general.  An adversarial model designer will still
> be able to trash any general init scheme.
>
> Here's the example from the salm model, with some ill-behaved
> random inits:
>

messages.subject: get_base1()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was profiling the epil model, and noticed that a huge amount of time
was being spent in std::string! It turns out that this is a result of
converting from const char*s to const std::string&s when calling
get_base1() like so:

get_base1(BT,n,"BT",1);

If the third argument is a const std::string&, then what happens is
the std::string constructor gets called, a std::string gets created,
and then it gets destroyed when you leave the function. This is a lot
of work to do for every array access! (A really smart compiler would
realize that this work is unnecessary, but apparently g++ isn't quite
that smart.)

I've pushed a change that replaces those const std::string&s with
const char*s, which leads to a 2–3x speedup for epil. I'm happy to
roll it back, though if someone thinks there's a reason to.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] get_base1()
messages.body_plain:
Awesome!  That should make all the models faster.

The reason all that get_base(...) stuff is there
is in order to deal with the std::vector vs.
Eigen::Matrix accessors.  It's all to make things
work out so that you can get a row of an Eigen
matrix using [] notation in Stan.

I'm really hoping the inlining is working here so that
the actual calls to get_base() aren't expensive -- it's
a static lookup as to which one gets called.

An alternative would be to add the following operator
overload method to Eigen's Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>:

    template <typename T>
    Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> operator[](int n) {
        return a.get_row(n);
    }

Daniel -- do you know if that's possible given the way
they let you add functionality?

It would have the added benefit of generating much
easier-to-read code.

- Bob

I just pushed a change to stack_alloc.hpp that streamlines alloc() and
should make memory allocation significantly more efficient. The old
version was sufficiently complicated that it wasn't actually getting
inlined (at least by g++ 4.2), which results in a big performance hit.
For example, the new version is about 23% faster on rats, which
corresponds almost exactly to the amount of time the profiler said it
was spending in stack_alloc::alloc().

Matt

I'm always surprised by what's fast and not.  If you
did what I was suggesting on the board (and earlier
on the list), I'd have thought the lack of virtual functions
would be a huge win.  That, and keeping all the data
a bit more local and having the code evaluated be very
tight.

The compiler/CPU/bus must be doing a very good job on the
virtual functions.  Maybe it can predict the branch
far enough ahead?  It's obvious in principle where you're
going.

 > But it did get me
> thinking about alternative ways of implementing agrad. Since almost
> all of our vari classes have to keep around pointers to their parents
> (or is it children?), we can formalize that and say that the base vari
> class has a vari* array pointing to its parents. To eliminate virtual
> function calls, you just add a vector
  of forward (backward?) adjoints
> that you compute in the constructor.

Reverse mode is from the root of the expression
tree down to the subexpressions.

 > Then the chain() function is
> completely generic, it just looks like
>
> for (int i = 0; i<  nparents_; i++)
>    parents_[i]->adj_ += adj_ * forward_adj_[i];

This is similar to what you wrote the first time.
I changed it the first time because it's not
space optimal and I thought space would be a huge
problem.  It's actually not going to be nearly as bad
as I thought because almost all of those iterative
matrix algorithms have derivatives that are more of
the same, so we won't usually have to pass agrad::var through
iterative algorithms like eigenvector solvers.

But it's not space optimal.  Consider operator+(var,var).
You'd wind up storing two copies of 1.0 in forward_adj_ and
then doing a multiply by 1.0 you don't need.

We'd also need to store nparents_, which presumably could
be a byte or maybe a short, but given byte alignment issues,
will probably be more expensive.  In the OO approach, it's
implicit in the vtable, which is only stored once.

But in some cases it is space optimal.  Having a vari
implemented this way will play nicely anyway.

Then if you go and put the parents and the adjoints onto
their own stacks rather than storing vari at all,
you're back to my other proposal you said didn't save
much in time (though I understand this is for ease of
programming).

> Even if it's not faster, I think this approach actually simplifies
> specializing vari a little bit, since you don't have to mess around
> with all of the op_vd_vari op_vv_vari op_dv_vari etc. etc. etc.
> classes; all that matters is the number of varis that get passed in.

Right -- the logic goes to the operator itself, which
is much cleaner in that the derivative code is close
to the operator code.

> I
> wonder if some sort of similar abstraction could be useful in getting
> around the 2**K issue. I'm envisioning templated versions of each vari
> class where you only compute the forward adjoints for the arguments
> that are varis. Something to think about, maybe. It'd be kind of nice
> to not have 7 fma() implementations cluttering up
> special_functions.hpp.

I've been thinking the same thing recently.
It's not optimal, as you sometimes don't need
to store a double arg to compute the gradients.
An example is operator+(double,var&), for which
you only need to store the var.

It's also problematic type-wise.  At least I
can't figure out a workaround.

First, assume you have two wrapper functions:

   inline double getval(double x) { return x; }
   inline double getval(var x) { return x.val(); }

For simplicity, assume we're storing a var rather
than vari*.  The var is just a pointer to implementation
anyway.  (It might've been cleaner to do it that way
all around if the compiler could optimize away the
field access to the vari* inside a var.)  We could get
the vari* with some fancy metaprogramming footwork to
pull out the type and value of storage: double for double
and vari* for var.

The class would look like this:

template <typename T1, typename T2>
class add_vari : public vari {
    T1 a_;
    T2 b_;
    add_vari(T1 a, T2 b)
      : vari(getval(a) + getval(b),
        a_(a),
        b_(b)
      { }
    void chain() {
       if (is_var<T1>::value) a_.vi_.adj_ += adj_;
       if (is_var<T2>::value) b_.vi_.adj_ += adj_;
    }
}

This also isn't space optimal. Looking at operator+()
again, you'd need

No problem with the metaprogram for the condition,
but the body of the if statements only make sense
if the object is a var.

Aha.  Now I think I see how to do it!  Nothing
like writing it out again.  Another template

   static double DUMMY;

   double& get_adj(double x) { return DUMMY; }
   double& get_adj(var& x) { return x.vi_.adj_; }

and then the chain() method becomes:

    void chain() {
       if (is_var<T1>::value) get_adj(a) += adj_;
       if (is_var<T2>::value) get_adj(b) += adj_;
    }

All the bogus get_adj(double) will never be called
because the metaprogram is_var<double>::value will
evaluate to false.

This is where I got stuck last time, but I think
this hack is workable.  Even if the code's not
optimal, often you do need all the values (like with
operator*(T1,T2)), and there's our coding time.

- Bob

messages.subject: eigen 3.1
messages.body_plain:
Eigen is proposing to release 3.1 in a couple of weeks, whereas stan embeds eigen 3.0 . I don't know when we should try to upgrade. Obviously, we aren't currently using any 3.1 features (which are primarily related to official supporting of formerly unsupported modules on sparse matrices, nonlinear optimization, and various backends), so maybe stan 1.0 should ship with eigen 3.0 .

The way stan/lib is organized does not lend itself to testing with the system's eigen, mostly due to including the unsupported FFT module. I think it might be better to have

stan/lib/eigen

include all of the eigen tarball except the stuff we delete. And then have the makefile pass

-I lib/eigen/Eigen -I lib/eigen/unsupported/Eigen .

That way someone like me could just change that line of the makefile to

-I /usr/include/eigen3/Eigen -I /usr/include/eigen3/unsupported/Eigen

to see what if anything would break (the same could be said for versions of Boost).

Ben

messages.subject: new auto-dif faster on simple example
messages.subject_clean: new auto-dif faster on simple example
messages.body_plain:
(Discussion moved to stan-dev.)

I just ran a very simple example (multiplication, code below)
and the new auto-dif runs a bit more than twice as fast!

     Old vs. New Impl
     ----------------
                   Old Impl   New Impl
     clang++ -O3      1.00s      0.61s
     g++     -03      0.77s      0.37s

     Optimization Level (New Impl)
     ---------------------------
     clang++           g++
     -O0: 4.67s        3.01s
     -O1: 1.67s        0.46s
     -O2: 0.61s        0.37s
     -O3: 0.61s        0.37s
     -O4: 0.67s        0.37s

This is encouraging enough to implement more and run some
more tests.  First, I'm going to see if using std::vector
has any performance impact.

We were already faster than the main open-source auto-dif
implementations for C++, CppAD and Trilinos.

What also has me a bit geeked is that I think I can do
something like what CppAD does to deal with threading in
such a way there'll be a small constant performance hit
for each gradient calc, but nothing like the per-var cost
of using the old system with thread local stacks.

Here's the code for the two tests:

Old Code
--------

   double total = 0.0;
   for (int i = 0; i < 20000000; ++i) {
     var a = 5;
     var b = 6;
     var c = a * b;
     grad(c.vi_);
     total += a.adj() + b.adj();
     recover_memory();
   }

New Code
---------
   double total = 0.0;
   for (int i = 0; i < 20000000; ++i) {
     var a = 5;
     var b = 6;
     a.set_independent(); // DIFF
     b.set_independent(); // DIFF
     var c = a * b;
     c.calculate_gradient();
     total += a.adjoint() + b.adjoint();
     recover_memory();
    }

The main difference is the set_independent()
call (before any use of the vars) that tells the
system that var a and b are variable and not
constants.  The default constructor used in "var a = 5"
[or "var a(5)"] will create a constant.

Now that I said that, I noticed that there is some
inefficiency in using a = 5 -- you get a copy and
a constructor, and now copies are more expensive.  So
I changed the first four lines in the loop to:

     var a(5,true);  // construct as independent
     var b(6,true);

and it reduced the g++ -O3 time (all we care about
from now on [as Matt has told us all along]) to .29s
(from .37s).  Not that this will help much in the
generated Stan code in most cases.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] understanding C++ optimizations -- extra code runs faster
messages.body_plain:
A well predicted branch could be cheaper than indirect memory access.
Computing adjoints[node_] involves fetching node_ (whose location is
known and can be prefetched) and then fetching adjoints[node_] (whose
location is not). is_constant() only requires a single fetch from a
known location, so might be easier to pipeline. Could be some
speculative evaluation going on as well—if is_constant() turns out to
be true, then you can just keep going and don't stall waiting to get
adjoints[node_].

This is, of course, all highly speculative. But none of it is
inconsistent with the adage—it's much faster not to run "return
adjoints[node_];".

Matt

messages.subject: bad news on heap vs. program memory
messages.subject_clean: bad news on heap vs. program memory
messages.body_plain:
Matt put his finger on why std::vector was slow
compared to the current static allocations:

     const int MAX_NODES = 1000000;
     double adjoints[MAX_NODES];
     int edges[MAX_NODES];

If I change the above to use heap data, as in

     double* adjoints = new double[MAX_NODES];
     int* edges = new int[MAX_NODES];

then the new auto-dif isn't any faster than the
original one -- it might even be a bit slower.

Is there a better way to have dynamically configurable
sizes?  I was thinking if there was a better generic
way to do this, std::vector would be using it.

I might be able to make it a bit faster by
combining some of these things into structs
so there aren't as many accesses.

I really don't want to have to hard-code sizes
into the generated code for the model (what would
be required to have this both be static and
configurable at least at code-generation time).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] bad news on heap vs. program memory
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] bad news on heap vs. program memory
messages.body_plain:
Bah. That's disappointing.

I don't think there's any way to do dynamic allocation that doesn't
involve the heap. Unless we were interested in trying to come up with
some inline assembly that hacks the stack. Which would be a fun, but
dangerous (and probably doomed) exercise.

Or, we could conceivably do something with dynamic linking.
Specifically, we could make a bunch of agrad.so files each of which
has a different value of MAX_NODES, and swap them in and out whenever
we need more space. (Doing the necessary memcpying to preserve state.)
This would open the whole awful can of worms of dynamic linking, of
course, in addition to being kind of a pain in other regards. But at
least it's safer than manipulating the stack pointer by hand!

Anyone else have any bad ideas?

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] dynamic share objects of libstan and libstanc
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] dynamic share objects of libstan and libstanc
messages.body_plain:
Just because everybody else does something doesn't mean it's a good
idea for us. As I see it, there are a couple of reasons to use shared
objects:
1. if you're building a library that will be used by a number of
programs that will run simultaneously (e.g., libc) then it's a little
wasteful to duplicate that library's object code in memory for every c
program you're running
2. if you want to be able to load compiled plugins at runtime, there's
no alternative to dynamic linking (by definition).

Neither of these are relevant for libstan or libstanc, at least for
the current state of stan, since I doubt there will ever be many
unique stan programs running simultaneously on any one machine, and
anyway the statically linked executables are well under 1MB. Honestly,
I think (1) is a much less compelling argument than it was when
computers had MB instead of GB of memory. It's still important for
things like libc (mostly for cache reasons), but I can't imagine it
being too relevant for libstan.

The major downside to using shared objects is that the program has to
be able to locate those shared objects at runtime. This means that,
for example, you can break the program just by moving it to a
different directory. (Unless you've installed libstan and libstanc in
some appropriate directory like /usr/local/lib, which I'd rather not
require.) If you've ever had a missing dll error when you tried to run
a windows program, you've been hit by this problem.

Basically, my feeling is that dynamic linking is something that should
be steered well clear of if there's not a very compelling reason for
it. They call it "dll hell" for a reason. But if someone feels
differently I'd be happy to hear an argument to the contrary.

Matt

runtime rather than compile time means that it can be a command-line
option, like java's heap space. If we overrun the maximum number of
items (which should happen fast), we can print an error message saying
exactly how to change the command line. Or, we can have it be an
"advanced" option, where the default is to use a dynamically allocated
var stack but you can specify a fixed size var stack.

Bob and I were discussing adding a constructor into Eigen's DenseBase
class. The answer is yes.

be extended using which preprocessor directives):
http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/TopicPreprocessorDirectives.html

Something that got us earlier is that the declaration for the plugin
has to be declared before the first time Eigen is included. In other
words, include order matters in this case.

messages.body_plain:
There's a fairly high cost to wrapping double
in a var.  In the case where I use program variables
(NOT heap), and where a and b are variables, we have:

   f(a,b)          Speed
   -----           ---------
   a*b             new system 50% faster
   5.0*(a*b)       neck and neck
   2.0*(5.0*(a*b)) old system 25% faster

And at this point, the trend's pretty clear.

I was thinking we could use the same trick to do a light
wrap of a double in a var for the old system with

var
    double val_;
    vari* vi_;

We could then check (vi_ == 0) everywhere and just
deal with val_ in those cases.  But it looks like it's
going to be expensive:  it's mainly the ctor, the fact
that var is heavier than double, and also the branching.

Using heap memory is about the same cost as using
std::vector by the way -- not surprising given how
well class member access gets compiled.

- Bob

> I think with any approach we would still want to special case mixed operations to speed things up.

Absolutely!

 > The advantage being
> that we wouldn't be required to implement every possible combination for every operation.

That's already what's going on in the to_var() functions
in agrad/matrix.hpp -- they promote double-based vectors and
matrices to stan::agrad-based ones.  It's just even more expensive
to wrap the current version of var than the new one because of the way
memory is always allocated on the auto-dif stack.  This is why there's
so much incentive to vectorize and specialize the templates in
what we have now.

Adding the kind of wrapper I'm talking about now would have
a vari* pointer set to 0 for "constant" agrad::var instances.
Then every operation is going to have to test != 0 and
do something different in the two cases.  In the current
implementation, it's all static decisions.

bread-and-butter logistic regressions, most of the ops
are mixed.

messages.body_plain:
On 6/14/12 6:44 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 >
 > I'd agree with Markus that it would be nice if we could make these decisions after we get mixed type operations into
 > master.

Matt compared three options for evaluating normal_log
in the BUGS Rats model:

    1. current implementations (no vectorization)

    2. vari subclasses for normal_log(T_y,T_loc,T_scale)

       : this does the partial eval of gradients
         and thus cuts down on the expression graph
         size

    3. vectorized vari subclass for normal_log(vector<T_y>,vector<T_loc>,T_scale)

       : this further cuts down the expression graph
         size and can save repeated log calcs on scale param

Cutting down the expression graph size is a HUGE win.
Each node in the graph corresponds to a subexpression
and requires

    (a) memory allocation + constructor call,

    (b) value chasing to values through the vari* pointers, and

    (c) virtual function calls for applying the chain
        rule function chain() for each expression.

Matt's 1--3 and its related transforms and densities do
not use Eigen at all (at least I don't think they do).

At various times we've tinkered with trying to get
mixed type operations into Eigen itself (first I tried,
then Ben made some more progress). By mixed operations,
I mean binary vector operations where one argument is
double and one is agrad::var.

    4.  mixed operations

        : this will mean we don't need to wrap double vectors
          in var vectors and cuts down on (a) and (b)

I also think the mixed ops will let us take advantage of
their expression templates, which will cut out some of
the intermediate copies.  I don't think this is causing
us huge overhead, but inasmuch as we copy matrices, it involves
some C++ heap ops, which are relatively slow.

We're already OK on the complex things like solvers, because
those are working on homogeneous agrad::var types.  It's
the mixed operations in things like the transforms and
some of the other multivariate densities that would be helped most.

I think the question is then whether having mixed ops in
Eigen would help us carry out the kind of optimizations
Matt did in (3).  That is, we could have something like a
mixed (y - mu) operation for double vectors y and variable vectors mu.
This would certainly help any C++ code involving mixed operations
as indicated in (4) above.   And any vector operations users
wrote directly in Stan.

Matt's optimizations go one step further, though, and directly
compute the gradients for

    normal_log(double* y, var* mu, var sigma);

with respect to sigma and the components of mu.  There's only
one node in the expression graph corresponding to this normal_log
function (just like there's one node for multiplication).  Having vectorized
diffs isn't going to help with that, because you still wind
up building a big expression graph when all the individual
sums and products are called on the doubles and vars in y and mu.

Mixed ops will definitely help with more ad-hoc Stan code,
too, that doesn't make use of vectorization (in the sense
of normal(double*,var*,var)) but does use vector operations.

The kind of mixed-op implementation Markus did for dot product
will be faster (because it's an instance of (3) above) than
just putting mixed operations into Eigen itself.

The really interesting design question is whether we could lean
on some of the expression templates themselves and reimplement
them to do smarter, more compound things with their variable
arguments.

One place we might use expression templates right away is
in the log_prob += pattern that's going on everywhere.  We
might be able to squeeze some compile-time vectorization out
of that by building up a sum-of-terms expression template.

Whew.

- Bob

messages.subject: best of both worlds!
messages.body_plain:
Summary:  I figured out how to implement with our current
auto-dif single function for densities like normal_log that handles
both propto and all eight combos of templates that evaluates about 4
times faster than the current approach.

All we really needed was a bunch of vari implementations
constructed with the partials along with another sprinkle
of template metaprogramming.

I should be able to get it all integrated with Stan later
today.  It's a little tricky to do without introducing
a dependency from stan::prob to stan::agrad.

I still haven't figured out how to generalize over scalar
and vector inputs efficiently in a single function.  An
inefficient way to do it would be to automatically proote
all the non-vectors up to vectors using an expression template
and then do all the definitions for vector-like objects.

Otherwise, I think we could probably get away with a less
than full set of vectorizations.  For instance, for normal_log,
I think we really only need:

     normal_log(scal,scal,scal)
     normal_log(vec,scal,scal)
     normal_log(vec,vec,scal)
     ?? normal_log(vec,vec,vec)
     ?? other 4 versions

Is there any case where there are varying locations but a
fixed outcome? Or any case we need vectorized scales?

In any case, we could implement each vectorized version as
a single function the same way I just did normal_log.

messages.subject_clean: split R-hat in variogram and autocovar for ESS
messages.body_plain:
We're looking at setting up the samples object and
also evaluating speed, so we need to compute ESS.

We're using the split chain R-hat to measure convergence.
Then the split chain estimate of var^+.

QUESTION: Should we put the chains back together to measure
autocovariance, or just do that on split chains, too?

Here's what I added to the to-do for speed testing:

Speed Comparisons (vs. JAGS)
======================================================================

* Run JAGS compiled with g++ -O3

* Look at models where Stan performs well
   e.g.  logistic or linear regression w. Cauchy and Normal prior
   - varying model shapes (step up exponentially)
     + number of data items
     + number of parameters
     + correlation of parameters (multi-variate Cauchy or Normal)
     + interaction of params (? need this with correlation ?)
     + conjugate vs. non-conjugate priors
       (well and misspecified -- more stats than speed issue)

* Single threaded

* Run 4 chains (each of same length) of each system (Stan and JAGS)
   - diffuse initializations (hand generate for each)
   - until convergence by split R-hat (all params under 1.05)
   - total (across all chains) ESS is > 100 (and < 150 or something?)
     (e.g., 25/25/25/25, or 15/35/20/30)
   - report time in effective samples/second of min ESS param

* Report multiple runs of each (10? 100?)
   - histograms/densities or mean/sd of multiple runs
   - how much will it vary by seed

* Throw away first half of each run?
   - to start, until split convergence/sample speeds

* Ideally, measure:
   - time to converge to equilibrium
   - ESS rate at equilibrium

- Bob

I patched stan::io::dump_reader so that it can handle
more general R dump output.

Now you can use R's colon notation, so that
"2:4" is equivalent to "c(2,3,4)"
and "4:2" is equivalent to "c(4,3,2)".

You can also use R's explicit "L" or "l", so that
"7", "7L", and "7l" are all equivalent.

I also updated the doc.

- Bob

This is mainly going to matter in the case where someone
wants to unfold the derivative calcs rather than using
auto-diff.  It makes a big difference in speed.

At that point, we have a coding style in play that'll
make it pretty clear in a way rather like the Rcpp interface
to the R data structures:

1.  pull values out in double-based scalars, vectors, etc.
     using value_of() function.

2.  compute log probability and derivative, dropping terms
     based on include_summand<> metaprograms and dropping
     gradient terms based on is_constant<>.

3.  return by calling something like simple_var(value,y,dy,mu,dmu,sigma,dsigma);
     [that function needs a better name, like partials_var].

What we're talking about now is mostly about how to
save ourselves a combinatorial explosion in writing
simple_var() and the underlying support class in the
face of variable/double/vector of variable/vector of double,
etc. arguments.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vectorization etc.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've pushed a new branch called "vectorized" to github that implements
full vectorization/specialization for the normal in a way that should
hopefully be reasonably easy to port to other distributions (or other
functions). It includes a version of rats called rats_vec.stan that
demonstrates one way to take advantage of the vectorization. This new
version takes about 3.2 seconds to generate 10000 samples (plus 1000
warmup samples), compared to the previous (partially vectorized)
version's 4.4 seconds. By contrast, my handwritten autodiff-free
implementation of rats takes about 1.65 seconds. And JAGS takes about
1.3 seconds (although a lot of that's inefficient I/O). In summary:
JAGS		1.3
handwritten	1.7
fully vectorized	3.2
partially vec'ed	4.4
unspecialized	19.1
We've come a long way towards eliminating our autodiff overhead in the
past few weeks!

Bob, we can talk about merging this into the main branch tomorrow, perhaps?

messages.body_plain:
Quick update: turns out that a minor change to rats_vec.stan actually
makes it significantly faster. The new version only takes 2.6s on
rats.

Also, if I comment out the body of check_range() and the calls to
check_finite() etc. then that goes down to 2.1s. So we're currently
paying something like a 25% overhead for that safety. It'd be nice to
have a way to disable at least the bound checking as a command line
feature, but it's surprisingly tricky to implement; the issue is that
you basically need two compiled versions of the model, one doing bound
checking and the other not. Which probably means significantly longer
compile times, which might not even be worth it.

Anyway, the main point is that we're capable of getting within about a
factor of 2 of JAGS's efficiency on its home turf (very low
correlation between parameters and full conditional conjugacy).

Matt

On Jun 24, 2012, at 10:30 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:

> Right, it should be easy to deal with at compile time. I was thinking

> but that may not be practical. Or all that important, come to think of
> it.

> On Sun, Jun 24, 2012 at 8:08 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> On Sunday, June 24, 2012 6:56:53 PM UTC-4, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>>
>>> Also, if I comment out the body of check_range() and the calls to
>>> check_finite() etc. then that goes down to 2.1s. So we're currently
>>> paying something like a 25% overhead for that safety.

You can save a bit of time by moving the checks out
of the loop so that the scale parameter is only checked once.
There are already vectorized versions that
should work on either values or vectors of values.

>>> It'd be nice to
>>> have a way to disable at least the bound checking as a command line
>>> feature, but it's surprisingly tricky to implement;
>>> the issue is that
>>> you basically need two compiled versions of the model, one doing bound
>>> checking and the other not. Which probably means significantly longer
>>> compile times, which might not even be worth it.
>>

Right -- the disable-checks flag will have to be available at compile time.

>> I suspect the overhead is much worse for multivariate models. I think it is
>> easy to fold these checks into the same mechanism that Eigen uses to
>> {dis,en}able range checking, depending on whether -DNDEBUG is passed.
>>

NDEBUG is a built-in C++ macro for turning off asserts.  It's apparently
handled differently than other macros by the compiler in that it
can be redefined in a single translation unit.

The bounds checking in the distributions now is based on Boost's
math error handling pattern, which is not based on assert.  It's designed
to allow the behavior of compound functions to do the right thing (e.g.,
return NaN vs. throw an exception vs. write to an error log and return NaN, etc.)
So they're not set up with a way to be turned off.

If we turn these errors off, user code may segfault or just return NaN
depending on how the other functions behave in the face of illegal
inputs (e.g., sqrt of a negative number).

To turn off our checks if NDEBUG is defined, use

if (!NDEBUG) {
    … error checks ...
}

The main downside is that we can't now turn off Eigen checks
and leave our own in place.

Another alternative would be to add another template param
such as:

  template <… ,bool DISABLED = stan::error_checks_disabled>
  check_finite(…) {
      if (DISABLED) return;
  }

Then we just need to make sure stan::error_checks_disabled is
a static constant defined before the probability functions.

Of course, the template default for a function is a purely C++11 thing.

One option would be to move them all to be static class methods:

template <bool DISABLED = false>
class tests {
  static S check_finite(…) {
      if (DISABLED) return;
       ….
  }
};

Then the usage is, e.g., tests<DISABLED>::check_finite(….).
This is assuming we make all the tests just cover doubles
and not agrad::var.

In retrospect, it might've been better to do the probability functions
this way, too.   It would've saved us some redundancy.  It's not too late
to change, of course.  I think it might even make the usage neater,
as in:

  template <bool PropTo = false, typename Policy = default_policy>
  class normal {
    template <typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale>
    log_prob(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu, const T_scale& sigma) { … }
    cumulative_distribution(…) { … }
  }

- Bob

messages.subject: RStan preliminary plots
messages.body_plain:
I have implemented plot and traceplot in rstan.  See the attachments for what they look like.
Rplots (1),pdf is from another run, in which for some reason some
split R hats are larger. Currently, the values of Rhats is depicted by the color of the 80% intervals line
somehow --- black: < 1.2,  blue: < 1.5, green: < 2, red: >= 2 (or NaN).

Use the 8 schools as an example, here is the R code:

library(rstan)

dat <- list(J = 8,
            y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
            sigma_y = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18),
            sigma_xi = 25);

s.f <- stan(file = "eight_schools.stan", data = dat, verbose = TRUE, n.chains = 3)

print(s.f)
plot(s.f)
traceplot(s.f)

This is what print(s.f) prints:

> print(s.f)
            Mean     SD    2.5%    25%    50%   75%  97.5%  Rhat      ESS
mu         6.227  4.231  -1.540  3.301  6.280 8.936 14.790 1.009  354.285
xi         1.375 13.866 -27.662 -6.314  0.665 8.518 31.182 1.022  187.893
eta[1]     0.031  0.788  -1.593 -0.306  0.018 0.374  1.652 1.002  913.220
eta[2]     0.034  0.689  -1.536 -0.238  0.037 0.296  1.617 1.016  290.896
eta[3]     0.035  0.780  -1.488 -0.290  0.010 0.294  2.096 1.001  419.660
eta[4]    -0.015  0.670  -1.334 -0.305 -0.015 0.246  1.315 1.004 1012.663
eta[5]    -0.031  0.662  -1.521 -0.333 -0.015 0.263  1.335 1.003  861.803
eta[6]    -0.009  0.794  -1.610 -0.308 -0.008 0.299  1.710 1.003  667.843
eta[7]    -0.047  0.851  -2.233 -0.314  0.006 0.323  1.445 1.007  293.423
eta[8]     0.048  0.813  -1.604 -0.282  0.003 0.326  1.909 1.001  499.884
sigma_eta  0.668  0.569   0.136  0.297  0.504 0.810  2.294 1.158    5.354

By the way, this is the 8 schools stan code
(file stan/src/models/misc/eight_schools/eight_schools.stan):

// EIGHT SCHOOLS MODEL

data {
    int(0,) J;               // number of schools
    real y[J];             // estimated treatment effect (school j)
    real(0,) sigma_y[J];   // standard error of effect estimate (school j)
    real sigma_xi;         // prior scale (coefficient)
}
parameters {
    real mu;               // intercept coefficient (for y)
    real xi;               // slope coefficient (for y)
    real eta[J];           // predictor (school j)
    real(0,) sigma_eta;    // deviation of eta
}
model {
    sigma_eta ~ cauchy(0,1);
    for (j in 1:J)
        eta[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_eta);
    mu ~ normal(0,10);
    xi ~ normal(0, sigma_xi);
    for (j in 1:J)
        y[j] ~ normal(mu + xi * eta[j], sigma_y[j]);
}

--
Jiqiang

messages.body_plain:
Awesome!

What's up with the second run?  Was the lack of mixing due
to a different seed?  I may not have specified the model properly.

Some comments:

1.  Could we get a title with the name of the model.  The titles and
legends on the graphs themselves all look great.

2.  A time stamp for the run (date/time)

3.  For the print, is there a way to print the command-line
parameters?  I'm mainly concerned with users being able to
report what they did and to recreate it if they need to.
I don't think this'll be necessary for the plots.  But if we
want to produce a single PDF report, I suppose it could all
go together:  model definition, parameters, print results,
plots.

4.  Is there a way to pack the graphs that don't
need so much space?  I was thinking a horizontal
rather than a vertical layout would be nice.

mu       --------x--x---------
xi
eta[1]
eta[2]
...
eta[8]

5.  Right now, we can't see the individual chains.  Can we plot
them all one above the other, as in:

mu   chain1    --------x-----------
      chain2 ----------x---------
      chain3       --------x--------
      chain4     ------x---------

xi   chain1  ....

Each would get its own x axis label, of course.

The chains could be packed very close and if we use color, the
chains themselves won't need labels.  But I don't know
how to color-code each chain AND indicate dodgy R-hat values with
color.  Maybe use the R-hat to shade the name of the variable,
add a warning symbol, or shade the background?

6.  I think the crosses are too busy.  I think a single line perpindicular
to the axis would be easier to scan.  So that'd really be

mu   chain1    --------|-----------
      chain2 ----------|---------
      chain3       --------|--------
      chain4     ------|---------

7. If we're going horizontal, we can probably use some space to report
R-hat.  One option is the name of the variable itself.

8. If the names of variables are too long, it could be arranged as

      sigma_eta_transformed_value
      ------|--------------------
        ---------|------------

9.  We probably need a non-PDF output format like PNG.
The 300KB files take forever to scroll on the Mac in Preview
and will do the same to PDFs in which they're embedded.

10.  The shading of warmup is great.  It may need to be a bit
higher contrast.  I think we're converging well before 1000 samples.

11.  No red+green palates -- they don't work for the color blind.
(And a lot of us area
ggplot2 has some good color palates built in.

12.  I don't like that all the samples are ruled differently.
For instance, mu has 6 divisions and eta only 3.  Any idea why
that is?

13.  Should the various eta[1] ... eta[8] have the same limits?
Right now, they vary a lot.  In unscaled regression problems in
general you might get a lot of variance, so I'm not sure what the
right default is.  The merging of limits on the left-hand-side of
the current R2WinBUGS plots is what makes those useless.

14.  I wouldn't mind seeing the median line and 80% intervals on
the traceplots.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RStan preliminary plots
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the comments.

Some answer to Bob's questions:

> 1.  Could we get a title with the name of the model.  The titles and
> legends on the graphs themselves all look great.
> 2.  A time stamp for the run (date/time)
> 3.  For the print, is there a way to print the command-line
> parameters?

All three are fine.

> 4.  Is there a way to pack the graphs that don't
> need so much space?  I was thinking a horizontal
> rather than a vertical layout would be nice.

It is difficult to manipulate lots of little plots so that they are packed without
much space in some cases.  In my opinion, ggplots' managing layout of
a bunch of plots is even worse than the often used (or old)
R graphics.  Currently I am using another package (gridExtra) to finally
lay out the plots for all parameters; but I can only set
# of rows and # of cols and then each plot occupy one cell.
Now I am using 4 and # of rows and 1 as # of cols.  (If someone
knows a better approach, please let me know).  The other reason
is that we sometimes have parameters like beta[N, M,..].

> 5.  Right now, we can't see the individual chains.  Can we plot
> > them all one above the other, as in:
> > mu   chain1    --------x-----------
> >     chain2 ----------x---------
> >     chain3       --------x--------
> >     chain4     ------x---------
> > xi   chain1  ....
> > Each would get its own x axis label, of course.
> > The chains could be packed very close and if we use color, the
> > chains themselves won't need labels.  But I don't know
> > how to color-code each chain AND indicate dodgy R-hat values with
> > color.  Maybe use the R-hat to shade the name of the variable,
> > add a warning symbol, or shade the background?

I will try to pack the information about chains.  But it is not easy
to control all elements as I wanted and sometimes you just cannot.

> 6.  I think the crosses are too busy.  I think a single line perpindicular
> to the axis would be easier to scan.  So that'd really be
> mu   chain1    --------|-----------
>     chain2 ----------|---------
>     chain3       --------|--------
>     chain4     ------|---------

Absolutely agree with you.

> 7. If we're going horizontal, we can probably use some space to report
> R-hat.  One option is the name of the variable itself.

I think horizontal is better.  I am using vertical only because that is
in the right side of plot from R2WinBUGS.  I am happy to
change that as Andrew did not say no to this comment.

> 8. If the names of variables are too long, it could be arranged as
>     sigma_eta_transformed_value
>     ------|--------------------
>       ---------|------------
> 9.  We probably need a non-PDF output format like PNG.
> The 300KB files take forever to scroll on the Mac in Preview
> and will do the same to PDFs in which they're embedded.

I am just using pdf to show the results and it is automatically generated by
running the R code as a script.  The output is controlled
by the user.  It could be in png, pdf, or on the screen.

>
> 10.  The shading of warmup is great.  It may need to be a bit
> higher contrast.  I think we're converging well before 1000 samples.

>
> 11.  No red+green palates -- they don't work for the color blind.
> (And a lot of us area
> ggplot2 has some good color palates built in.

I am happy to change that.  Actually, even now user can change them
as I made them configurable.

>
> 12.  I don't like that all the samples are ruled differently.
> For instance, mu has 6 divisions and eta only 3.  Any idea why
> that is?

I do not know.  I guess for example for 1 to 7, 6 divisions is better.  And for
1 to 4, 3 is better.  So I think I would still leave that to ggplot.

> 13.  Should the various eta[1] ... eta[8] have the same limits?
> Right now, they vary a lot.  In unscaled regression problems in
> general you might get a lot of variance, so I'm not sure what the
> right default is.  The merging of limits on the left-hand-side of
> the current R2WinBUGS plots is what makes those useless.

Andrew told me yes if I understood correctly. I know in some cases, it is a terrible idea to group
all them together.  And actually, it makes arranging all the plots difficult since
plots have different number of lines. But sometime, it might be good since we
can compare them.  Actually, now we could plot them in another way
by specify parameters in plot functions.  That is, if say beta is a vector of
length 8.  plot(sf, pars = "beta') will group all 8 beta together.
And we can do
plot(sf, pars = c("beta[1]", "beta[2'])).
The latter would take beta[1] and beta[2] separately.

> 14.  I wouldn't mind seeing the median line and 80% intervals on
> the traceplots.

Overall, this is a good idea.  But sometime it is not since if the initial values
are too scattered, the trace plots are almost lines.  In this case,
I do not know if we need come up a better way to do the traceplots.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RStan preliminary plots
messages.body_plain:
I re-organized to put the ones Andrew might be interested
in at the top.  I'm very excited you've gotten so far with this.
It would've taken me forever to do it.

On Jun 25, 2012, at 9:56 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:

> > 5.  Right now, we can't see the individual chains.  Can we plot

> > > them all one above the other, as in:
> > > mu   chain1    --------x-----------
> > >     chain2 ----------x---------
> > >     chain3       --------x--------
> > >     chain4     ------x---------
> > > xi   chain1  ....
> > > Each would get its own x axis label, of course.
> > > The chains could be packed very close and if we use color, the
> > > chains themselves won't need labels.  But I don't know
> > > how to color-code each chain AND indicate dodgy R-hat values with
> > > color.  Maybe use the R-hat to shade the name of the variable,
> > > add a warning symbol, or shade the background?
> I will try to pack the information about chains.  But it is not easy
> to control all elements as I wanted and sometimes you just cannot.

We should talk to Andrew about this issue.  Now that I look closely
at the R2WinBUGS output, I see that the left-hand plots (the one with
R-hats) and the right-hand plots are very different (there's an example
in BDA, p. 594).

Left side:  chains stacked above one another
                  no mean/median marked
                  variables all share same x axis scale
                  there are r-hats plotted from 1 to 2+

Right side:  chains on top of each other
                              (or are the 80% intervals from pooling chains?)
                     multivariate variables arranged horizontally
                               (always in a 1 x N grid, no matter the dimensionality)
                     medians indicated with colored dots per chain

I sort of like being able to see the r-hats plotted as they
are (next to the quantiles in a horizontal layout).

The right side is too wasteful of space, which is why I think
the horizontal plots stacked is the way to go.

Overall background shading could work to
to indicate problematic R-hat values.  Contrast may be an
issue.   (See color palette comment below.)

We need a different scale for each parameter.  When
deviance gets plotted (as it does by default in R2WinBugs),
the other parameters' intervals shrink to dots.

Is the packing a technical issue with ggplot2?  Have you tried
faceting for the chains?

I'm happy to jump in and help with fine-tuning the look and
feel.

> > 12.  I don't like that all the samples are ruled differently.
> > For instance, mu has 6 divisions and eta only 3.  Any idea why
> > that is?
>
> I do not know.  I guess for example for 1 to 7, 6 divisions is better.  And for
> 1 to 4, 3 is better.  So I think I would still leave that to ggplot.

How are you judging better here?  I'm guessing they're
preferring round numbers on the ticks.

This is another issue I know Andrew feels strongly about (but
I'm not sure if he has general advice as opposed to case-by-case
advice).

13.  Should the various eta[1] ... eta[8] have the same limits?
> > Right now, they vary a lot.  In unscaled regression problems in
> > general you might get a lot of variance, so I'm not sure what the
> > right default is.  The merging of limits on the left-hand-side of
> > the current R2WinBUGS plots is what makes those useless.
>
> Andrew told me yes if I understood correctly. I know in some cases, it is a terrible idea to group
> all them together.  And actually, it makes arranging all the plots difficult since
> plots have different number of lines. But sometime, it might be good since we
> can compare them.  Actually, now we could plot them in another way
> by specify parameters in plot functions.  That is, if say beta is a vector of
> length 8.  plot(sf, pars = "beta') will group all 8 beta together.
> And we can do
> plot(sf, pars = c("beta[1]", "beta[2'])).
> The latter would take beta[1] and beta[2] separately.

We can bring this up in the meeting, too.  I'm also not sure
what the right thing to do is.

This may be another issue that ggplot2 can sort out for us
with faceting in a single plot.  The issue is then how to group
parameters.

> > 14.  I wouldn't mind seeing the median line and 80% intervals on
> > the traceplots.
>
> Overall, this is a good idea.  But sometime it is not since if the initial values
> are too scattered, the trace plots are almost lines.  In this case,
> I do not know if we need come up a better way to do the trace plots.

We could always switch to a log scale, though that'd
probably confuse people.  Otherwise, the only thing
I could imagine doing was plotting them separately,
but that would be confusing because of the different scales.

Is it easy to configure to include the warmup or not?

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now for the rest of the comments that I don't think we
need Andrew for (unless he has issues with color, which
is the next topic).

> > 11.  No red+green palates -- they don't work for the color blind.
> > (And a lot of us area
> > ggplot2 has some good color palates built in.
>
> I am happy to change that.  Actually, even now user can change them
> as I made them configurable.

Nice.  There is some kind of palette selection in ggplot2.
We should just choose a default that prints well, has high
enough contrast, and no major red/green issues.

We want a "qualitative palette" for the chains and a
"sequential palette" for the R-hat values.  I'd vote for
Set2 for qualitative.

If we are going to do R-hat by shading the background,
maybe the central values of the reversed RdBu palette.

For more info, see:

http://blog.ggplot2.org/post/24607351280/choosing-colour-palettes-part-ii-educated-choices

> > 4.  Is there a way to pack the graphs that don't
> > need so much space?  I was thinking a horizontal
> > rather than a vertical layout would be nice.
>
> It is difficult to manipulate lots of little plots so that they are packed without
> much space in some cases.

I know.  I wouldn't worry about this so much to start.
We can work on packing tighter later.

> In my opinion, ggplots' managing layout of
> a bunch of plots is even worse than the often used (or old)
> R graphics.  Currently I am using another package (gridExtra) to finally
> lay out the plots for all parameters; but I can only set
> # of rows and # of cols and then each plot occupy one cell.

I think this'll be easier with horizontal layouts.  (I don't even
know how to do that in R.)

> Now I am using 4 and # of rows and 1 as # of cols.  (If someone
> knows a better approach, please let me know).  The other reason
> is that we sometimes have parameters like beta[N, M,..].

I think we can just stack the beta[N,M,…] cases on top of each other.

But once we get to hundreds of parameters, I don't think putting
everything in one big graph will be feasible.

> > 9.  We probably need a non-PDF output format like PNG.
> > The 300KB files take forever to scroll on the Mac in Preview
> > and will do the same to PDFs in which they're embedded.
>
> I am just using pdf to show the results and it is automatically generated by
> running the R code as a script.  The output is controlled
> by the user.  It could be in png, pdf, or on the screen.

Ah, right.   We'll just need to give people advice on how
to generate them.

- Bob

Although I agree with the philosophy of "release early, release often (and listen to your customers)", I think it is less essential for a header-only project with a public git repository. Anyone who knows about and wants to use Stan has been able to do so for a while, so I doubt there are that many people who are waiting for the code to be blessed with a 1.0 before they go ahead with their project.

> Now that Jiqiang's made so much progress on the R interface,
> it also brings up the issue of whether to wait for that.

If there are a substantial number of people that want to use Stan but aren't currently, they are probably people that feel they need an interface to facilitate things. So, I think rstan is worth waiting for.

> Now that Matt added a slick vectorization pattern for normal,
> should we add the other distributions?  (This'd take me around
> a week or so, though Daniel and I could split the work and do
> it faster.)

If we are going to wait for rstan (or for any other reason), then I think harmonizing the pattern for the distributions would be good. Another thing is the question of whether to upgrade / test Eigen 3.1 now that it is released.

> regression model with improper priors as:

...

> This does bring up the issue of writing a faster matrix-vector
> multiplication implementation for (x * beta) along the lines
> of what Marcus did for dot products (it'd basically use
> the dot products in the output cells).

Anything that can simplify the syntax of the .stan files is great. The idea that a user has to write the model as a text file is probably the biggest hurdle to overcome for people who don't write a lot of code. I think the stan syntax is already simpler than WinBUGS while simultaneously offering more features, but incorporating the vectorization would constitute even more progress on both fronts.

Ben

messages.subject: Bug in data file parsing
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick note, I've stumbled on a bug in the data file format parsing.  In particular, if you have something like the following:

foo <- 4
loo <- 10

the variable loo will not get parsed correctly.  Rather it will get parsed as "oo".  The beginning 'l' will be dropped.  This is probably due to the logic which is trying to parse the number 4 on the previous line and recognizes a trailing l or L. messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] mcmc::chains' get_samples method
messages.body_plain:
On 6/26/12 11:23 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> In mcmc::chains, we have the following get_samples, which merged the samples for a parameter from all
> chains including warm up samples.

get_samples() on line 719 of chains.hpp does not merge
-- it only returns the samples for a single chain.

> I do not think we need such a function.

We were going to let users get the results by chain.

We want to implement all the user functionality, at least
to the extent possible, on the C++ side.  The main motivation
is to keep the code size on the client (R) side down so
that it's easier to port to Python and Matlab and whatever
else people might want.

 > Instead, we could have
> get_kept_samples(size_t n, std::vector<double>& samples),
>
> which merges the samples for all the chains assuming samples after warming up are good.

We have get_kept_samples_permuted() on line 774.
It merges across chains AND applies a permutation.
The same permutation gets saved and used for all
parameters.

There's no matching un-permuted get_kept_samples function.

This is because Andrew wanted to apply a permutation
to the returned samples after they're merged to
protect users from themselves.

If you want something from the R side that returns
the kept samples without permuting them, we can take it up
again with Andrew.  (I also may have misunderstood his
intent.)

> I think I could do the change if my thought is right.

If you just need something on the C++ side, by
all means, go ahead and add it.  I'm happy to take
a look at it after you do if you'd like.

- Bob

messages.subject: check validity of object created from Rcpp module
messages.subject_clean: check validity of object created from Rcpp module
messages.body_plain:
I am forwarding a question I asked on Rcpp dev list.  Due to limits of Rcpp and the answer I got,
I have to say that in our current implementation and design, the underlying c++ mcmc chains
object for our fitted stan model could not be saved and then loaded to another R
session.  And if loaded, the end-user could have error or even segfault; the segfault
could would end the R session.  So most of our fitted stan model could live in only one R session.

--
Jiqiang

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Dirk Eddelbuettel <e...@debian.org>
Date: Tue, Jun 26, 2012 at 8:04 PM
Subject: Re: [Rcpp-devel] check validity of object created from Rcpp module
To: Jiqiang Guo <guo...@gmail.com>
Cc: rcpp-...@lists.r-forge.r-project.org

On 26 June 2012 at 17:21, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
| Dear List,
|
| I am wondering if there is a way to check whether an object created from Rcpp's
| module is valid or not especially for objects loaded in another session.
|
| In detail, we know that we could not save and load objects created from Rcpp's
| module [section 5 of http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Rcpp/vignettes/
| Rcpp-modules.pdf].  But that does not prevent users doing that. So if an
| object created from Rcpp's module is loaded in another session, we would end up
| with errors or even segfault.  It would be nice we have a method to check if
| it is valid or not so that when we are writing a package, we could do a check
| before calling those methods of that object.

It's a very good idea. I don't have a good idea as to how we'd do this though.

Dirk

| An illustrative example:
|
| require("Rcpp")
| require("inline")
|
| inc <- '
| class Foo {
| private:
|   int x_;
| public:
|   Foo(int x) : x_(x) { }
|   int getx() const { return x_;}
| };
|
| RCPP_MODULE(foo) {
|   class_<Foo>("Foo")
|   .constructor<int>()
|   .method("getx", &Foo::getx)
|   ;
| }
|
| fx <- cxxfunction(signature(), "", include = inc, plugin = "Rcpp", verbose =
| FALSE)
| m <- Module("foo", getDynLib(fx))
| cppo  = new(m$Foo, 5)
|
| print(cppo$getx())
| save("cppo", file = 'cppo.RData')
|
| rm(list = ls())
| load("cppo.RData")
| print(cppo$getx())
|
| For the above code, we know the last line would not work.  If we have a
| function to test the validity of cppo,then if not valid, we would not call
| cppo's function and are able to tell users that cppo is not valid any more.
|
| Best,
| Jiqiang
|
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------
| _______________________________________________
| Rcpp-devel mailing list
| Rcpp-...@lists.r-forge.r-project.org
| https://lists.r-forge.r-project.org/cgi-bin/mailman/listinfo/rcpp-devel
--
Dirk Eddelbuettel | e...@debian.org | http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com

messages.subject: Matrix multiplication optimization
messages.body_plain:
I've just checked in some code to further speed up matrix multiplication and push the dot_product_vv_vari-style classes a little further into the Eigen stack.  There are two distinct changes here.

1) dot_product_v[dv]_vari member functions which operate on Eigen types now take Eigen::DenseCoeffsBase<Derived> types instead of the previous Eigen::Matrix<var,R,C> types.  This allows the mutliply() functions to use ConstRowExpr and ConstColExpr types, in effect avoiding copying each row and column into a temporary array before constructing the dot_product varis.

2) I've provided specialized implementations of Eigen::internal::general_matrix_vector_product and Eigen::internal::general_matrix_matrix_product for the matrices of vars which uses a new dot_product_vv_vari-like class.  This is important because internal Eigen operations (e.g., factorizations, solving linear systems, etc) can end up doing matrix products which bypass our multiply() routines.  It may be possible to take this approach even further by specializing gebp_kernel for var type matrices.  Further, this code is not completely optimized, as it doesn't do the memory sharing that multiply() and dot_product_vv_vari do.

Also, on a related note, I highly recommend using cachegrind for profiling.  The first change above provided a ~20% speedup on my model but I never would have thought of doing it except I looked at the profile results.  It turned out ~15% of execution time was being spent just on memory allocation/deallocation, most of which was happening in multiply().

Cheers,
Marcus

> On Fri, Jun 29, 2012 at 2:54 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I'll check out cachegrind.
> >
> > Nice to see more of the template expressions being pushed through.
> >
> > The only issue now is that the unit tests are broken,
> > at least on the Windows server.  Here's a link to the
> > error novel:

> > http://d1m1s1b1.stat.columbia.edu:8080/job/Stan%20Unit%20Tests/1224/console
>

>
> I'll take a look.
>
> >
> >
> > On 6/29/12 2:37 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> > > I've just checked in some code to further speed up matrix multiplication and push the dot_product_vv_vari-style classes
> > > a little further into the Eigen stack.  There are two distinct changes here.
> > >
> > > 1) dot_product_v[dv]_vari member functions which operate on Eigen types now take Eigen::DenseCoeffsBase<Derived> types
> > > instead of the previous Eigen::Matrix<var,R,C> types.  This allows the mutliply() functions to use ConstRowExpr and
> > > ConstColExpr types, in effect avoiding copying each row and column into a temporary array before constructing the
> > > dot_product varis.
> >
> > That's nice.  The copies themselves probably aren't so expensive but
> > all the messing around with memory under the hood for Eigen (and std::vector
> > in other cases) can be a killer.  But the only way to avoid the heap
> > is if you know the sizes at compile time, which we don't (and I believe
> > Eigen ignores it anyway if it's beyond a certain size).
>
> Actually, I think there's been enough other optimizations that, at least according to my profiling, the memory allocation and copying were hurting a fair bit.  I suppose this is a good sign as things like chain() are starting to show up near the top of the profile.
>
> >
> >
> > > 2) I've provided specialized implementations of Eigen::internal::general_matrix_vector_product and
> > > Eigen::internal::general_matrix_matrix_product for the matrices of vars which uses a new dot_product_vv_vari-like
> > > class.  This is important because internal Eigen operations (e.g., factorizations, solving linear systems, etc) can end
> > > up doing matrix products which bypass our multiply() routines.
> >
> > The problem we've always had in the past trying to do what you
> > suggest in (2) is all the intermediate templates not being
> > defined.  I don't know if that's related to the error above.
>
> Those internal specializations are basically just the core routines that Eigen calls after all the intermediate templates are evaluated and actually do the calculations.  The expression templates shouldn't play into it all.
>
> >
> >
> > > It may be possible to take this approach even further by
> > > specializing gebp_kernel for var type matrices.  Further, this code is not completely optimized, as it doesn't do the
> > > memory sharing that multiply() and dot_product_vv_vari do.
> >
> > OK.  Ben's looked at some of this.
> >
> >
> > > Also, on a related note, I highly recommend using cachegrind for profiling.  The first change above provided a ~20%
> > > speedup on my model but I never would have thought of doing it except I looked at the profile results.  It turned out
> > > ~15% of execution time was being spent just on memory allocation/deallocation, most of which was happening in multiply().
> >
> > Thanks for the pointer.  I'll take a look.
> >
> > - Bob
>

Everything ran fine in clang++ 2.9 on Mac OS X.

g++ 4.2.1 was having a problem with anonymous namespaces,
so I just changed the name of a structure and it shut up.

Unfortunately, agrad/.../inv_wishart is up to its old tricks.

~/stan>make CC=g++ O=0 test/agrad/distributions/multivariate/continuous/inv_wishart

   src/stan/prob/distributions/multivariate/continuous/inv_wishart.hpp:94: error: no matching function for call to
   ‘mdivide_left_tri(Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var, -0x00000000000000001, -0x00000000000000001, 0,
   -0x00000000000000001, -0x00000000000000001>&, Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var, -0x00000000000000001,
   -0x00000000000000001, 0, -0x00000000000000001, -0x00000000000000001>&)’

...

I'm not sure why it's not matching.  Here's the signature
from agrad/matrix.hpp (there are all versions of var/double):

    template<int TriView,int R1,int C1,int R2,int C2>
     inline Eigen::Matrix<var,R1,C2> mdivide_left_tri(const Eigen::Matrix<var,R1,C1> &A,
                                                      const Eigen::Matrix<var,R2,C2> &b) {

At one point, I thought we were going to change those to
hard code in the upper or lower triangular bits.  So I went
ahead and added an mdivide_left_tri_low() w/o the TriView template
param and inv_wishart (and the other multivariates using mdivide_left)
work just fine.

g++ takes forever on my little Macbook Air, but when it's done,
I'll push the fixes.

- Bob

messages.subject: mcmcplots
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan crew,

Congratulations on your work on Stan. We're very excited about what it means for the future of Bayesian modeling.

We see that you've been working on your own graphing code for MCMC output. We have an R package, mcmcplots, that may be relevant at this stage.

mcmcplots has some pretty useful MCMC graphing functionality, including plots of chain trace, density, autocorrelation, and caterpillar plots. It's fast, and has a host of neat features. For instance, given an object of multiple chains of multiple parameters, it can save PNG images for each parameter and collate the images into an HTML file with a table of contents. This makes for a fast visual way of sanity-checking the output of a complex run.

Attached is a screenshot of one of the mcmcplots outputs. This is a combination of trace, density, and autocorrelation into a single image. The vertical bars on the density indicate 95% CIs for each of two chains, red and blue. The plot is of a parameter delta[1], and the plot title is displayed using the greek letter delta.

The code is here: https://github.com/s-mckay-curtis/mcmcplots . You're welcome to simply use the code on open source terms, of course, but we'd also be happy to work with you to add the functionality you need to mcmcplots. Please let us know if you'd be interested in working with us so mcmcplots can grow to suit Stan.

P.S. If you'd like to kick the tires, please use the code from github. A new release including some bug fixes is imminent, but has not yet happened.

Best regards,
S. McKay Curtis and Ilya Goldin
